Alright children, let's stop and watch for a moment. Here we have a perfect example of strawman propaganda. This is where the proponent of an idea supposes to take the position of their critics and then attack their own contrived arguments. It's as easy as beating a scarecrow with a stick!

Most proponents of GMO hail it as a panacea that could solve world hunger. We already know that we could solve world hunger if it weren't for vested interests and the powers that be. I don't know what GMOs, specifically pesticide resistant organisms, would do differently. Even if they would make every starving village in Africa self-sufficient, nothing is stopping the local warlord to usher in a new age of feudalism under the threat of violence.

What I'm getting at, is that the organizations in favor of GMO are citing altruistic motivations. When big corporations are spear-heading a movement to make the world a better place, I don't think that's what they're really intending to do.

And if pesticide resistant crops would yield so much more than what we are producing now that would mean that current practices (conventional, because it's not GMO vs. organic yield) is losing a lot of the harvest to pests. I have no idea which numbers, but even if pesticide resistant crops could drive that loss down to less than 1%, and current loss was, say, 20%. That still wouldn't make such a difference in pricing, even if the loss was higher than 20% (which I don't think is the case). Because let's compare it to conventional vs. organic yield. This paper says that organic yields 95% best case to 66% worst case, of what conventional yields. So for starters there is an obvious mark up for most organic products since they can fetch for twice the amount of its conventionally grown equivalent. Even still, the pricing difference is not something that would cause economic tidal waves. And the same will probably hold for pesticide resistant crops.

Thirdly, I don't think that creating a solution to a problem that only addresses the symptoms rather than the cause is good practice, despite being standard practice. Things like the Gros Michel banana becoming commercially unsustainable in the '50s due to monoculture farming, or how papaya on Hawaii is protected from a virus with a GMO version of papaya, again due to monoculture farming. These are the prime examples of why agriculture businesses first sell us the problem then sell the solution. Maybe the way we mechanized agriculture is the most optimal way in terms of yield, in the short run. And it surely is more efficient than pre-industrial methods. But maybe having a huge combine harvesters mowing away on fields of a single crop as far as the eye can see isn't the most sustainable in the long run. And perhaps not that much more profitable than polyculture on an industrial scale. But I guess in a free market capitalist society that will be how things are run.
